analysis.one_liner: Requires food makers to disclose old self-certified "safe" ingredients for FDA board review.
analysis.headline: A bill to make food companies disclose ingredients they self-certified as safe before 2000 — many never seen by the FDA — was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on January 30, 2026 and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, food companies can declare an ingredient "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS) on their own, without ever telling the FDA. This bill targets designations companies made before 2000 that were never filed with or reviewed by the agency: within 90 days of the law taking effect, manufacturers would have to list them for a new government review board. The board would review the designations, and if it finds an ingredient has not been shown to be safe, the Secretary of Health and Human Services could revoke the designation and require the product to be pulled from shelves.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers gain the most: thousands of food ingredients on the market today rest on safety judgments companies made about themselves, sometimes decades ago, without the FDA ever seeing them. The bill forces those ingredients into the open and gives the government power to remove any that cannot be shown to be safe. The FDA and USDA also gain a structured process and new enforcement tools, including civil penalties and the ability to treat an undisclosed ingredient as an unapproved — and therefore illegal — food additive.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a review board, run through HHS and FDA with USDA and EPA participation, that must examine every pre-2000 GRAS designation a company made without notifying the FDA, categorize them by priority, and publish its findings on the FDA website.

Forces food manufacturers to disclose, within 90 days of enactment, every covered GRAS designation they hold — the first time many of these self-certifications would ever reach the government. Companies that refuse face civil penalties or having their ingredient treated as an unapproved, unsafe food additive.

Lets the Secretary revoke a designation the board finds unsupported, giving the manufacturer 180 days to produce real safety evidence, and requires procedures for pulling and recalling substances that fail — closing the gap where an untested ingredient could otherwise stay on shelves indefinitely.

Sunsets the whole program after 10 years and requires public reports to Congress at set deadlines (2 years for the highest-priority tier, 4 for the next, 10 for the rest), so the review has a defined endpoint and a public paper trail.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers bear the cost. They must identify and disclose their legacy GRAS designations within 90 days, submit to board review, and — if a designation is revoked — either produce scientific safety evidence within 180 days or stop distributing and recall the substance. Failing to disclose brings civil penalties under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or treatment of the ingredient as an unapproved food additive. Those compliance, reformulation, and recall costs would ultimately be partly passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The 90-day disclosure deadline is extremely tight. Companies would have to identify designations made as far back as before 2000 — including by predecessors or acquired brands — and incomplete or late filings could trigger penalties even for companies trying to comply.

The review board is made up almost entirely of government officials, with only one non-voting industry representative and one non-voting academic food toxicologist. With no dedicated funding or staffing provisions in the bill, reviews of potentially hundreds of designations could be slow — the lowest-priority tier has up to 10 years — and the board sunsets after 10 years, so some substances could go unreviewed before the program ends.

If designations are revoked, companies must cease distribution and recall products, which raises costs and could pull familiar ingredients off the market. Supporters would argue that is the point — unproven ingredients should not stay on shelves — but it is a real cost, and one an honest backer should acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: a large share of the food supply relies on safety determinations companies made about themselves without FDA review, and this bill would finally surface and test them. The costs fall on food manufacturers in compliance, possible recalls, and reformulation, with some passed to consumers as higher prices. The design is imperfect — a 90-day disclosure deadline is likely too fast for decades-old records, and the 10-year sunset means the slowest-priority reviews might never finish — but the core trade favors the public: proving an ingredient is safe before it stays legal is a fair burden to place on the company profiting from it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it sits there while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Lawler (R-NY) introduced the GRAS Oversight and Transparency Act on January 30, 2026.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over food and drug law.
One House Democrat signed on as a cosponsor; no further action, hearing, or vote has occurred, and the 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has been changed by the bill: food manufacturers continue to rely on pre-2000 self-affirmed GRAS designations without disclosing them to the FDA, and consumers continue eating ingredients the government has never reviewed.

for.name: Rep. Michael Lawler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, directing HHS to create a board to review pre-2000 self-affirmed GRAS designations.

for.name: 1 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one Democratic and one Republican sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 30, 2026; the committee has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor recommendation.

against.name: Food manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long defended the self-affirmed GRAS process that this bill would force into review; no public position on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes to measure, but early support crosses party lines: a Republican sponsor with one Democratic cosponsor, and no recorded opposition yet.

industries.note: The bill ends the quiet use of pre-2000 self-affirmed GRAS designations: companies must disclose them, submit to review, and face revocation, recalls, and civil penalties if an ingredient cannot be shown to be safe. Because these companies profit from ingredients whose safety was never independently checked, their financial interest runs against the stricter review consumers get.

Suppliers of legacy additives face the same disclosure, review, and possible recall requirements, and a revoked designation would take their products off the market unless safety is proven within 180 days. Consumers gain an independent safety check on ingredients they currently cannot verify.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive. But it is a backbench pattern: a single sponsor with one cosponsor, no committee hearing or markup more than a sit in committee, and referral to a committee with a crowded agenda. Absent either a markup or attachment to a larger food-safety or appropriations vehicle, the likeliest path is that it dies quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027.
